section_1.title: Prerequisite: Defining the Planar Graph
section_1.content: Define a planar graph as a graph that can be drawn on a plane without edges crossing. Introduce the basic components: Vertices (V), Edges (E), and the new concept of Faces (F)—the distinct regions enclosed by edges, including the infinite outer region.
section_1.example: Visualizing a 'Spiderweb': A complex web is planar if it can be rearranged on a flat surface so that no two silk threads intersect.

section_2.title: Euler’s Characteristic Formula
section_2.content: Introduce Euler's formula: V - E + F = 2. Explain that this is a topological invariant for all connected planar graphs. Use a step-by-step animation showing how adding a vertex or edge maintains the balance.
section_2.example: Start with a simple triangle (V=3, E=3, F=2): 3 - 3 + 2 = 2. Add an edge to split one face: V=3, E=4, F=3; 3 - 4 + 3 still equals 2.

section_3.title: The Concept of Graph Duality
section_3.content: Explain how to construct a Dual Graph (G*): Place a vertex in each face of the original graph G. Connect two dual vertices if the corresponding faces share an edge. Show the 'mirror' relationship between the two graphs.
section_3.example: Imagine a 'Cell Map': A floor plan of a house (original) can be turned into a 'Connectivity Map' (dual) where each room is a node and each door is an edge.

section_4.title: Connecting Euler and Duality
section_4.content: Demonstrate the mathematical relationship: V* = F, E* = E, and F* = V. Show how Euler’s formula holds for the dual graph, reinforcing the symmetry between faces and vertices in planar structures.
section_4.example: Using a 'Chessboard': If the squares are vertices, the dual graph creates a grid pattern that maps the center-to-center movement of a knight.

section_5.title: Real-world Application
section_5.content: Briefly mention applications in VLSI circuit design (minimizing wire crossings) and map coloring (Four Color Theorem foundation). Summarize the beauty of topological properties.
section_5.example: A circuit engineer using Euler's formula to ensure that a chip layout can be printed on a flat board without short-circuiting connections.
